summary_en: One full orbit of 5553.6 s on a two-body circular orbit at 400 km altitude was sampled at 1 s intervals including the end-of-period instant, giving 5555 instants; the satellite position, the Earth-centre-to-Sun vector and G were all taken from the Orbit output, with 2159 instants in eclipse umbra and 16 instants in penumbra. prepare_surface_environment was called at every instant for 7 constructed attitudes, namely the identity quaternion, 90° rotations about each of the three axes, an arbitrary composite rotation, and a random unit quaternion and its negative, and also for the torque-free rigid-body attitude from the Orbit attitude dynamics EulerDynamics and an Earth-pointing attitude constructed instant by instant from the orbit position, 49995 calls in total; 13 hand-calculated geometry examples were also run. In the Earth-pointing attitude the body Z axis points to the local zenith and the radiator face RAD_mZ faces the Earth centre; the solar array front-face normal is the body X axis, taken as the projection of the satellite-to-Sun direction onto the local horizontal plane, and the incidence cosine of the solar array front face over the orbit ranges from 0.003399 to 1.000000. Compared with an independently written quaternion rotation matrix formula, hand results by axis permutation, the product of the three elementary rotation matrices, the Rodrigues rotation formula and the analytic expression of the Earth-pointing attitude, cos_incidence has a maximum error of 7.8×10^{−16}, meeting the criterion of no more than 1×10^{−12}. All surfaces facing away from the Sun receive negative values: 19 in the hand examples, 127765 over the orbit for the constructed attitudes and 31402 over the orbit for the two orbital attitudes, 159186 values in total, with a minimum of −1.000000. The incidence cosine computed with the Earth-centre-to-Sun direction differs from the result computed with the satellite-to-Sun direction by up to 3.6×10^{−5}, far larger than the criterion, which shows that the comparison can distinguish the two Sun directions. The returned dictionary contains the seven fields run_id, time_s, surface_ids, G_W_m2, cos_incidence, albedo_W_m2 and infrared_W_m2; the run identifier and time match the input, the arrays of the seven surfaces have equal length, their order is the same as the asset surface order, and the albedo and infrared inputs correspond surface by surface. G_W_m2 is bitwise identical to the sun_intensity output in all 49995 calls; it is 0 W/m^{2} at umbra instants and 29.1 to 1354.1 W/m^{2} at penumbra instants, identical to the Orbit output, so the function does not apply an eclipse factor again; when 1372.1 W/m^{2} without eclipse is input at umbra instants the function returns it unchanged, so the eclipse is counted only once, by Orbit. 51 invalid inputs were injected. The invalid inputs listed in the case include non-normalized quaternions and normals, a zero difference between the satellite position and the Sun vector, an unconverted TEME position, an unsupported coordinate frame, misaligned surface identifiers and a missing earth_flux record; following the general convention of Section 6.1, further inputs were added: inconsistent run identifier or time, satellite position, Earth-centre-to-Sun vector, quaternion and albedo arrays of wrong dimension, non-finite values in time, satellite position, Earth-centre-to-Sun vector, quaternion, G, albedo and infrared, and an epoch missing its time zone, missing a field or not of type datetime; negative G, albedo and infrared irradiances were also added. All these invalid inputs were rejected with deterministic errors, each error names the specific field, and repeated calls give the same error; the input data and parameters are unchanged before and after the call, and the function produces no temperature.
